claims.text: At high temperatures, high-entropy nanoalloy stability is governed predominantly by kinetically limited surface diffusion rather than solely by bulk configurational entropy.
The particles begin as well-dispersed, chemically homogeneous, single-phase solid solutions without phase segregation.
A surface-passivation coating inhibits surface diffusion.
Heating above approximately 800 °C activates surface and grain-boundary diffusion in the nanoalloys.
An inert or controlled atmosphere avoids extrinsic oxidation effects.
Surface atomic mobility and interface-driven diffusion can produce phase segregation or chemical ordering.
High-temperature exposure can cause initially solid-solution HEAs to decompose or develop multiple phases.
In unpassivated nanoparticles, high temperature enhances surface diffusion.
Enhanced surface diffusion weakens kinetic barriers at interfaces.
Lower interfacial kinetic barriers cause earlier phase segregation and chemical inhomogeneity.
Passivation increases the energy barriers for surface diffusion.
Suppressing surface diffusion preserves the bulk solid solution and improves structural stability at elevated temperature.
Relative to unpassivated particles, passivated particles will exhibit less phase segregation after equal heating durations.
Passivated particles will retain a more uniform elemental distribution and a more preserved phase structure than unpassivated particles.
The prediction is restricted to temperature regimes in which surface and grain-boundary diffusion are thermally activated, stated as typically above 800 °C.
The prediction may not apply when oxidation or other environmental effects dominate stability.
Thin inert oxide or nitride coatings are known to restrict surface-atom mobility.
Comparable segregation, diffusion rates, and loss of homogeneity in passivated and unpassivated particles would refute the claim that surface diffusion is the dominant stability-controlling factor.
